{{Short description|Mathematical theory}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Arakelov theory''' (or '''Arakelov geometry''') is an approach to [[Diophantine geometry]], named for [[Suren Arakelov]]. It is used to study [[Diophantine equation]]s in higher dimensions.

==Background==
The main motivation behind Arakelov geometry is that there is a correspondence between prime ideals <math>\mathfrak{p} \in \text{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})</math> and [[P-adic valuation|finite places]] <math>v_p : \mathbb{Q}^* \to \mathbb{R}</math>, but there also exists a place at infinity <math>v_\infty</math>, given by the [[Absolute value (algebra)|Archimedean valuation]], which doesn't have a corresponding prime ideal. Arakelov geometry gives a technique for compactifying <math>\text{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})</math> into a [[Complete variety|complete space]] <math display="block">\overline{\text{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})}</math> which has a prime lying at infinity. Arakelov's original construction studies one such theory, where a definition of divisors is constructed for a [[Scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] <math>\mathfrak{X}</math> of relative dimension 1 over <math>\text{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_K)</math> such that it extends to a [[Riemann surface]] <math>X_\infty = \mathfrak{X}(\mathbb{C})</math> for every valuation at infinity. In addition, he equips these Riemann surfaces with [[Hermitian metric]]s on [[holomorphic vector bundle]]s over ''X''('''C'''), the complex points of <math>X</math>. This extra Hermitian structure is applied as a substitute for the failure of the scheme [[spectrum of a ring|Spec('''Z''')]] to be a [[complete variety]].

Note that other techniques exist for constructing a complete space extending <math>\text{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})</math>, which is the basis of [[Field with one element|F<sub>1</sub> geometry]].

=== Original definition of divisors ===
Let <math>K</math> be a field, <math>\mathcal{O}_K</math> its [[ring of integers]],{{clarify|date=September 2026}} and <math>X</math> a genus <math>g</math> curve over <math>K</math> with a non-singular model <math>\mathfrak{X} \to \text{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_K)</math>, called an '''[[arithmetic surface]]'''. Also, let <math display="block">\infty: K \to \mathbb{C}</math> be an inclusion of fields (which is supposed to represent a place at infinity). Also, let <math>X_\infty</math> be the associated Riemann surface from the base change to <math>\mathbb{C}</math>. Using this data, one can define a '''c-divisor''' as a formal linear combination <math display="block">D = \sum_i k_i C_i + \sum_\infty \lambda_\infty X_\infty</math> where <math>C_i</math> is an irreducible closed subset of <math>\mathfrak{X}</math> of codimension 1, <math>k_i \in \mathbb{Z}</math>, and <math>\lambda_\infty \in \mathbb{R}</math>, and the sum <math display="block">\sum_{\infty}\lambda_\infty X_\infty</math> represents the sum over every real embedding of <math>K \to \mathbb{R}</math> and over one embedding for each pair of complex embeddings <math>K \to \mathbb{C}</math>. The set of c-divisors forms a group <math>\text{Div}_c(\mathfrak{X})</math>.

==Results==

{{harvs|authorlink=Suren Arakelov|last=Arakelov|year1=1974|year2=1975|txt}} defined an [[intersection theory]] on the [[arithmetic surface]]s attached to smooth projective curves over [[number field]]s, with the aim of proving certain results, known in the case of function fields,
in the case of number fields. {{harvs|txt=yes|first=Gerd |last=Faltings|authorlink=Gerd Faltings|year=1984|txt}} extended Arakelov's work by establishing results such as a Riemann-Roch theorem, a [[Noether formula]], a Hodge index theorem and the nonnegativity of the self-intersection of the dualizing sheaf in this context.

Arakelov theory was used by [[Paul Vojta]] (1991) to give a new proof of the [[Mordell conjecture]], and by {{harvs|txt=yes|first=Gerd |last=Faltings|authorlink=Gerd Faltings|year=1991}} in his proof of [[Serge Lang]]'s generalization of the Mordell conjecture.

{{harvs|txt=yes|first=Pierre |last=Deligne|authorlink=Pierre Deligne|year=1987}} developed a more general framework to define the intersection pairing defined on an arithmetic surface over the [[spectrum of a ring]] of integers  by Arakelov. {{harvs|txt=yes|first=Shou-Wu|last=Zhang|authorlink=Shou-Wu Zhang|year=1992}} developed a theory of positive line bundles and proved a [[Ample line bundle#Intersection theory|Nakai–Moishezon type theorem]] for arithmetic surfaces. Further developments in the theory of positive line bundles by {{harvs|txt|last=Zhang |year1=1993 |year2=1995a |year3=1995b}} and {{harvs|txt|first1=Lucien |last1=Szpiro |authorlink1=Lucien Szpiro |first2=Emmanuel |last2=Ullmo |authorlink2=Emmanuel Ullmo |last3=Zhang |year=1997}} culminated in a proof of the [[Bogomolov conjecture]] by {{harvs|txt|last=Ullmo |year=1998}} and {{harvs|txt|last=Zhang |year=1998}}.<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Leong |first=Y. K. |date=July–December 2018 |url=https://ims.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/imprints-32-2018.pdf |title=Shou-Wu Zhang: Number Theory and Arithmetic Algebraic Geometry |issue=32 |magazine=Imprints |pages=32–36 |publisher=The Institute for Mathematical Sciences, National University of Singapore |access-date=5 May 2019}}</ref>

Arakelov's theory was generalized by [[Henri Gillet]] and [[Christophe Soulé]] to higher dimensions. That is, Gillet and Soulé defined an intersection pairing on an arithmetic variety. One of the main results of Gillet and Soulé is the '''arithmetic Riemann–Roch theorem''' of {{harvtxt|Gillet|Soulé|1992}}, an extension of the [[Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch theorem]] to arithmetic varieties. 
For this one defines arithmetic [[Chow ring|Chow group]]s CH<sup>''p''</sup>(''X'') of an arithmetic variety ''X'', and defines [[Chern class]]es for Hermitian vector bundles over ''X'' taking values in the arithmetic Chow groups. 
The arithmetic Riemann–Roch theorem then describes how the Chern class behaves under pushforward of vector bundles under a [[proper morphism|proper map]] of arithmetic varieties. A complete proof of this theorem was only published recently by Gillet, Rössler and Soulé.

Arakelov's intersection theory for arithmetic surfaces was developed further by {{harvs|txt|first=Jean-Benoît|last=Bost|year=1999}}. The theory of Bost is based on the use of [[Green's function|Green function]]s which, up to logarithmic singularities, belong to the [[Sobolev space]] <math>L^2_1</math> (of [[L2 function|L<sup>2</sup> function]]s whose derivative is L<sup>2</sup>). In this context, Bost obtains an arithmetic Hodge index theorem and uses this to obtain Lefschetz theorems for arithmetic surfaces.

==Arithmetic Chow groups==
An '''arithmetic cycle''' of codimension ''p'' is a pair (''Z'',&nbsp;''g'') where ''Z''&nbsp;&isin;&nbsp;''Z''<sup>''p''</sup>(''X'') is a ''p''-cycle on ''X'' and ''g'' is a Green current for ''Z'', a higher-dimensional  generalization of a Green function. The '''arithmetic Chow group''' <math>\widehat{\mathrm{CH}}_p(X)</math> of codimension ''p'' is the quotient of this group by the subgroup generated by certain "trivial" cycles.<ref>Manin & Panchishkin (2008) pp.400–401</ref>

==The arithmetic Riemann–Roch theorem==
The usual [[Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch theorem]] describes how the [[Chern character]] ch behaves under [[Direct image of a sheaf|pushforward]] of sheaves, and states that ch(''f''<sub>&lowast;</sub>(''E''))= ''f''<sub>&lowast;</sub>(ch(E)Td<sub>''X''/''Y''</sub>), where ''f'' is a proper morphism from ''X'' to ''Y'' and ''E'' is a vector bundle over ''f''. The arithmetic Riemann–Roch theorem is similar, except that the [[Todd class]] gets multiplied by a certain [[power series]]. 
The arithmetic Riemann–Roch theorem states
<math display="block">\hat{\mathrm{ch}}(f_*([E]))=f_*(\hat{\mathrm{ch}}(E)\widehat{\mathrm{Td}}^R(T_{X/Y}))</math>
where
*''X'' and ''Y'' are regular projective arithmetic schemes,
*''f'' is a smooth proper map from ''X'' to ''Y'',
*''E'' is an arithmetic vector bundle over ''X'',
*<math>\hat{\mathrm{ch}}</math> is the arithmetic Chern character,
*''T''<sub>''X''/''Y''</sub> is the relative tangent bundle,
*<math>\hat{\mathrm{Td}}</math> is the arithmetic Todd class,
*<math>\hat{\mathrm{Td}}^R(E)</math> is <math>\hat{\mathrm{Td}}(E)(1-\epsilon(R(E))),</math>
*''R''(''X'') is the additive characteristic class associated to the formal power series <math display="block">\sum_{{m>0 \atop m\text{ odd}}} \frac{X^m}{m!}\left[2\zeta'(-m) + \zeta(-m) \left({1\over 1} + {1\over 2} + \cdots + {1\over m}\right)\right].</math>
